facts.statement: 将情景记忆操作化为时间、地点、实体及事件内容四元组的线索检索、实体最新状态及时间顺序；认知科学启发不等于测得人类主观回忆或海马机制。

method_function.text: 把记忆构念连接到可生成的任务及指标。

facts.statement: 正式比较分为完整书本in-context、RAG、GPT-4o-mini微调三路线；in-context六模型，RAG四个GPT/Claude模型，微调仅mini；模型/问题及生成器辅助检查不新增独立行为实验。

method_function.text: 明确模型×记忆方式的比较范围。

facts.statement: 静态宇宙每类100日期、全名、地点和内容，日期2024–2026，每内容30细节；Claude生成过量候选后去重筛选，随机日期/人名、打乱候选表并使用固定seed。

method_function.text: 构造可控且可重复抽样的合成世界。

facts.statement: 事件属性独立按截断几何分布抽样，p=.1，索引0–99，概率为(1-p)^i p/[1-(1-p)^100]；内容细节均匀抽样；拒绝重复(t,entity)或(t,space)，短20与长200使用同一候选前缀。

method_function.text: 提高多事件共享线索频率并约束事件唯一性。

facts.statement: 用10000次重复合成抽样比较几何/均匀分布下多匹配事件计数及SD；这是材料设计模拟，不是新增模型行为样本。

method_function.text: 评估材料生成分布的预期任务组成。

facts.statement: 每章段数均匀取1–10，属性安排到抽样段落，另抽写作风格；Claude-3.5-Sonnet-2024-06-20或GPT-4o-2024-05-13独立生成章节，日期地点主角事件细节须按指定段出现并使用次要角色占位符。

method_function.text: 以模板及位置约束控制叙事材料。

facts.statement: 先直接检查段落编号/数量、占位符、关键字所在段；通过后由同一生成器回答单地点/日期/主角/事件四个布尔问题；最多十次尝试后丢弃失败章节。

method_function.text: 过滤不符合结构化真值约束的生成材料。

facts.statement: 次要角色以500名和1000姓构造的100000名字池替换占位符且与主角名区分；两生成器各保留196/200章节，但被丢弃的四章不同。

method_function.text: 减少占位符及主次角色混淆并记录生成损耗。

facts.statement: 用经验累积分布检查属性在书本/章节/段落中的位置；整体书本章节较分散，但主角名偏段首。默认章节非时间顺序排列。

method_function.text: 检查位置分布并设置叙事呈现顺序。

facts.statement: 36模板中0–29为各种线索组合的回忆（含次要实体和整章详情），30–32最新状态，33–35实体时间轨迹；从结构化事件填槽建立真值并去重，完整详情真值为整章。

method_function.text: 构造多线索、多输出形式的已知答案问题。

facts.statement: 对每个事件每个属性以独立Bernoulli(.5)决定替换，分别从已有其他章节属性或未用宇宙属性抽替换值；每策略每章生成一次，再仅保留检索确实为空的问题。

method_function.text: 产生内域及外域不存在事件的阴性检索材料。

facts.statement: 目标按36模板×匹配章节数0/1/2/3–5/6+每格最多5题抽取，最多900；实际短456题、长686题。latest按相关章节数分箱而非单个最新答案长度；短章数有20/19差异，保留源冲突。

method_function.text: 用模板与匹配数量分层组成评测集。

facts.statement: in-context在专用系统提示下向模型提供整本书与问题，要求基于书本回答；六模型包括GPT-4o、mini、Claude-3-Haiku、3.5-Sonnet、Llama-3.1-405B-instruct及o1-mini。

method_function.text: 通过当前上下文提供可检索记忆输入。

facts.statement: RAG把章节/段落带ChapterX/ParagraphY标签嵌入text-embedding-3-small，以余弦相似度取top-K拼成上下文；默认段落，消融改章节且K=17（最大相关事件数）。默认段落K未明确。

method_function.text: 构造外部文本检索式记忆及粒度对照。

facts.statement: GPT-4o-mini用OpenAI微调，30epochs、batch64、learning-rate multiplier1.8；单事件QA长3199/短468。bin1明确训练与测试相同，其他bins仅测试。

method_function.text: 以权重更新记忆单事件，再检验多事件检索迁移。

facts.statement: 语义评审输出JSON identified_items及每个真值项的0/.5/1分；同义改述可满分，隐含相关可半分。提示规定答案含任意负面/不存在信息则identified_items置空，即使混有其他内容。

method_function.text: 把自由文本转为匹配项与部分语义得分。

facts.statement: 令S为真值匹配分之和、G为真值项数、I为回答识别项数；G>0时precision分母=min(I,G)，否则用I；recall=S/G，再算调和F1。此乐观分母可能忽略多余回答；空真值/零分母完整边界规则未明确。

method_function.text: 使用宽松集合检索准确性计分。

facts.statement: latest记完全匹配比例；时间顺序仅对真值长度≥2且整套事件完全匹配的回答计算Kendall τ。匹配提示按语义取尚未使用的最早真值索引，未匹配置-1、保持顺序并取共同项目；τ是成功检索条件下排序。

method_function.text: 分开事件找回与顺序一致性。

facts.statement: 示例说明语义评审可给部分分（GPT-4o约4%、mini约8%）；全文没有提供独立人类评分一致性或评审准确度研究，评审模型完整身份/参数也不足。

method_function.text: 披露自动语义评分的可核查范围。

facts.statement: 按问题计算F1均值±SD并按匹配事件数分箱；主排名用逐问题成对Wilcoxon signed-rank加Holm校正及临界差异图。书内共享事件/线索的依赖如何纳入推断未明确。

method_function.text: 比较模型路线的分层表现与成对统计差异。

facts.statement: 多匹配事件下表现明显下降；最新状态最高36%，完整事件集合≤18%。个别模型τ=1对应很少完整检索成功的答案，不能代表全局完美排序。

method_function.text: 描述记忆负荷及时间追踪困难的结果边界。

facts.statement: 附录分析书本长短、RAG粒度、线索数量/类型与输出轨迹；可用线索组合受唯一性约束，2+线索不都能产生多事件匹配，设计并非完全交叉。

method_function.text: 拆分任务结构和记忆接口对表现的影响。

facts.statement: 用GPT/Claude生成的短书比较四个in-context模型，使用单侧Mann–Whitney U；生成后的有效事件集合因丢弃项不同，无法认定严格成对相同章节材料。

method_function.text: 考察材料生成器选择的敏感性。

facts.statement: 将默认短书同一事件内容按时间顺序重排、保持问题，比较四模型；p=.23/.27/.40/.06均未达常用.05；表28还列ordered-long发布版本，未据此补造完整长书检验。

method_function.text: 检查章节呈现时间顺序敏感性。

facts.statement: 对196默认事件由LLM分五档可信性：100现实、7较现实、52有些不现实、31不现实、6不可能；合为R107/N89并把问题分empty/R-only/N-only/mixed。

method_function.text: 按事后材料可信性分层检查表现。

facts.statement: 可信性子组F1用单侧Mann–Whitney U比较，部分模型显著；子组关联不能证明现实性造成因果效应。

method_function.text: 比较材料属性与检索表现关联。

facts.statement: 人工检查GPT-4o的150个空答案问题中的24错误：17内域（14实体相关）与7外域（均时间线索）。此为指定错误案例分析，非全模型人工金标准。

method_function.text: 诊断内外域负例的混淆模式。

facts.statement: Gardner–Altman图对同题实验配对表现画连接线，并bootstrap模型间平均差；图中N=548，正文没有完整报告重采样次数、依赖单位或区间构造。

method_function.text: 展示配对差值及重采样分布。

facts.statement: Claude-3.5约342/685答案追加伪Human/Assistant对话；作者用包含尾部的整段回答评分。685与其他处长书686题不一致，所谓泄露微调指令只是作者解释。

method_function.text: 明确异常输出是否清洗及评价输入边界。

facts.statement: 另以Claude-3.5-Sonnet-2024-10-22生成新闻/科幻短长书；新闻450/697QA、科幻452/668QA。GPT-4o in-context仅简单回忆跨域评测，仍在2+事件下降。表28共11发布基准，含未报告模型测试的2000章约1M-token版本。

method_function.text: 检查跨叙事领域迁移并区分发布资产与实际测试。

facts.statement: 作者承认显式绝对日期、独立章节缺少因果联系、虚构类人领域及训练策略局限；相对时间、更真实互联事件、增强记忆机制与人类比较为后续方向。

method_function.text: 限制情景记忆构念及外推范围。

facts.statement: 作者声称合成世界按设计避污染；已供应全文没有直接检查被测模型训练语料的重叠审计。材料合成是实施方法，彻底无污染是未独立验证的主张。

method_function.text: 区分污染缓解设计与训练数据重叠证据。

evidence.quote:
Episodic memory – the ability to recall specific events grounded in time and space
– is a cornerstone of human cognition, enabling not only coherent storytelling, but
also planning and decision-making. Despite their remarkable capabilities, Large
Language Models (LLMs) lack a robust mechanism for episodic memory: we argue
that integrating episodic memory capabilities into LLM is essential for advancing
AI towards human-like cognition, increasing their potential to reason consistently
and ground their output in real-world episodic events, hence avoiding confabulations. To address this challenge, we introduce a comprehensive framework
to model and evaluate LLM episodic memory capabilities. Drawing inspiration
from cognitive science, we develop a structured approach to represent episodic
events, encapsulating temporal and spatial contexts, involved entities, and detailed
descriptions. We synthesize a unique episodic memory benchmark, free from contamination, and release open source code and datasets to assess LLM performance
across various recall and episodic reasoning tasks. Our evaluation of state-of-the-art
models, including GPT-4 and Claude variants, Llama 3.1, and o1-mini, reveals that
even the most advanced LLMs struggle with episodic memory tasks, particularly
when dealing with multiple related events or complex spatio-temporal relationships
– even in contexts as short as 10k-100k tokens.

Entities. Entities (entj ) are fundamental subjects in the world, that can participate in or be affected by
events: their attributes or relationships may change over time due to episodic events. More generally,
each entity has an associated state statej,t at any discrete time t. This state evolves based on events
and includes all details about the entity at a given time, such as its location and any observation such
as actions or interactions. The latest state of an entity is denoted as statej,L , where L denotes the
latest point in time.
Episodic events. Episodic events (eventi ) transcend the scope of the current benchmark, and
are defined as actions or observations that lead to changes in the state of the world or its entities,
including the mere progression of time. Specifically, each event eventi is characterized by a tuple
(ti , si , enti , ci ), where ti represents the time at which the event occurs, si the location where the
event takes place, enti the set of entities involved in the event, and finally ci corresponds to the
event content, detailing what happened. This formulation captures the essential elements of episodic
memory: what happened, where and when.
World model. This model of episodic events and entities aligns with the hippocampus’s role in
maintaining a dynamic cognitive map of the world. By tracking the states of entities across time
and space, our framework mirrors the brain’s process of continuously updating its representation of
the environment based on new experiences. This approach not only captures the context, space and
temporal properties of events, but also how these events transform our understanding of the world
and its constituents. In line with the encoding specificity principle (Tulving & Thomson, 1973), each
event is associated with specific details that differentiate it from others: parts of these details will
serve as retrieval cues during memory tasks. Now in LLMs, these episodic memory components are
represented as sentences or paragraphs describing the events, and entity states are inferred from the
context provided in the text.

We model cue-based recall as a key-value retrieval system, where the cue (key) is any combination of
elements from the event tuple (ti , si , enti , ci ), and the associated event details serve as the memory
trace (value). By systematically varying the cues, we can assess the model’s ability to retrieve specific
information based on different aspects of the events.

We start from a number of atomic components that we can combine to build possible worlds or

and a list of 30 details for each content. We ensured, when building them, that all the elements are
distinct. The Listing 1 provides an excerpt of such components.

We generate the components of the universe with the help of Claude 3.5 Sonnet. For reference, we

generate twice the number of targeted elements, and then to filter the duplicates and other incorrect

additional seed parameter is used for reproducibility.

Two constraints govern our actual generation. First, (i) we do not allow multiple events to have

# System prompt
You are a creative fiction writer specializing in detailed, atmospheric novel excerpts. Your task is to generate
vivid, immersive scenes based on specific prompts.
# User prompt
Write a detailed novel excerpt in a {style} style about {entity} attending a {content}.
The story takes place on {date}, at {location}, where {entity} {content_single_detail}.

Follow these guidelines:
Structure and Information Reveal:
1. Divide the text into {nb_paragraphs} paragraph(s). Number each paragraph (1), (2), etc., while
maintaining novel−appropriate paragraph lengths.
2. Gradually reveal key information:

As baseline models for our benchmark, we evaluate several LLMs, including GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini,
Claude 3 Haiku, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3.1 405B (instruct) and the recent o1-mini. We consider
memory in LLMs as functioning through three primary forms: (1) In-Context Memory, where
information is processed within the model’s context window; (2) Retrieval-Augmented Generation
(RAG), where external memory is accessed through a vector database; and (3) Parametric Memory
via Fine-Tuning, where memory is stored within the model’s parameters.
For (1) in-context memory, we prepend the full document to the question, allowing the model to
process the entire context. With (2) RAG, we chunk the book into paragraphs4 , each labeled with
context (e.g., "Chapter X, Paragraph Y"), and embed them using text-embedding-3-small. For each
question, we retrieve the top-K paragraphs based on cosine similarity to the question’s embedding
and prepend them to the question as context. Lastly, (3) we fine-tune models5 using all single-event
question-answer pairs as training data (details in Appendix B.2.5). In principle, this approach enables
models to acquire knowledge for all benchmark questions (including multi-event questions).

We use the main evaluation prompt defined in Listing 12 for deducing the F1-score between the
ground truth and the predicted answers.
The key idea is to adopt the ground truth point of view for performing the evaluation, since we are
sure of the number of ground truth items. In consequence, we assign for each ground truth item a
matching score between 0 (the item has been missing in the LLM predicted answer) and 1 (the item
has been found, considering synonyms or close meanings). In addition, we ask for the all identified
items in the AI answer, which is necessary to know the number of predictions, and hence assess false
positives.
B.3.2

C OMPUTATION OF THE F1- SCORE

The list of identified items iditems is not entirely controlled given the way it has been extracted.
There are numerous cases where its size is larger than the size of the ground truth, even for a coherent
AI-generated answer. For instance, (i) in the case of a full event, the ground truth is the full chapter
while the identified items may be a detailed list, (ii) in the case of the latest content, the ground truth
has size one while the identified items may include details about the different steps of the content
(as seen in the Listing 13), (iii) in the case of entity retrieval, the model may include the secondary
entities, that are not the protagonist but are still related. For those reasons, we decided to be lenient
in the number of predictions #pred and to define #pred = min (#iditems, #gt) if #gt > 0, and
#iditems otherwise. This policy is nevertheless straightforward to tune, since it does not rely on an
additional generative model. At the end, the sum of the matching scores S is the quantity that assesses
the number of true positives, from which the precision S/#pred and recall S/#gt are computed
(with #gt the number of ground truth items and #pred the number of predictions). The F1-score is
then computed as their harmonic mean.

S UMMARY AND LIMITATIONS

In this work, we draw inspiration from cognitive science to build a new episodic memory model for
LLMs, generate a comprehensive benchmark, and evaluate state-of-the-art models. Our findings
reveal significant gaps in the episodic memory capabilities of state-of-the-art LLMs, particularly
when handling multiple related events and complex spatio-temporal relationships. These challenges
reflect aspects of human memory where more distinctive cues facilitate easier retrieval. Furthermore,
naive finetuning fails to achieve a deep understanding of episodic events and their intricate relations,
merely overfitting to single learned facts. These challenges highlight the need for fundamentally new
approaches to model design and training that more closely emulate the dynamic and contextual nature
of the human episodic memory. The proposed episodic memory benchmark exhibits several desirable
properties: it is contamination-free by design, scalable with low human labor, offers unambiguous
cues and ground truth, and the ability to model multiple cues and events within a synthetic yet realistic
narrative. However, we acknowledge limitations that open avenues for future research.
Temporal representation. Our benchmark relies on explicit temporal markers, which may not fully
capture the nuanced ways time is expressed in natural language (e.g. “yesterday”, “last week”, or
“after the party”). Future iterations should incorporate implicit and relative temporal references to
further challenge the models.
Event independence. The independent generation of chapters, while facilitating control, does not
capture the interconnected and causal nature of real-world events.
Limited domain scope. Our benchmark primarily involves human-like protagonists within fictional
contexts. Extending the framework to include diverse domains (e.g., software projects, virtual
environments) would test models’ ability to generalize episodic memory capabilities.
Training limitations. The observed performance limitations suggest that current fine-tuning methodologies may not be optimally suited for episodic memory tasks, underscoring the need for developing
new strategies for the broad scientific community.

C OMPARATIVE EVALUATION BETWEEN REALISTIC AND NON - REALISTIC EVENTS

Our initial framework does not filter book chapters based on event plausibility. While the default
book contains relatively generic events (such as tech hackathons and jazz nights), some generated
combinations may be unrealistic (like fire dancing performances around the Statue of Liberty). We

adopt this approach since both LLMs and humans should be capable of reasoning about past, future,
and fictional episodic events, regardless of their realism. In the following section, we provide an
additional ablation study examining the impact of event realism on model performance.
Using the default long book generated by Claude (196 events), we employ an LLM-as-a-judge
approach to assess each event’s degree of realism. For each entry, we provide one representative
explanation:
• Realistic: 100 (Example: "This event is entirely plausible as it involves a common activity
(photography exhibition) at a real location (Port Jefferson) with a reasonable future date.
Photography exhibitions and workshops explaining post-processing techniques are regular
occurrences in art communities, and the timeframe (2026) is in the near future.")
• Moderately realistic: 7 (Example: "This event is moderately realistic because karaoke nights
are common social activities, and Chelsea Market is a real venue that could host such events.
Performing songs in different languages is also common in karaoke. The specific date in the
future and named person make it plausible, though we can’t verify if this exact event will
occur.")
• Somewhat realistic: 52 (Example: "While fashion shows in museums do occur occasionally,
and the American Museum of Natural History has hosted special events, it’s a relatively
unusual venue for a fashion show. The specific date in the future and named individual
makes it plausible, but museums focused on natural history aren’t typical locations for
fashion events compared to art museums or conventional fashion venues.")
• Non-realistic: 31 (Example: "This scenario is unlikely because Bethpage Black Course is a
prestigious golf course that wouldn’t typically allow parkour activities. Golf courses are
carefully maintained for golfing and would not permit activities that could damage the turf
or disturb golfers. Additionally, parkour typically requires urban structures or obstacles,
which wouldn’t be present on a golf course.")
• Impossible: 6 (Example: "Fire performances are strictly prohibited at the Statue of Liberty
as it’s a protected national monument with strict security measures. Additionally, visitors
are not allowed to perform any kind of shows or demonstrations inside or around the statue
due to safety regulations and preservation concerns.")

We observed that only a small number of events are non-realistic or impossible, but that even these
events would be plausible within the context of fiction.
Next, we further categorized the chapters into two classes:
• R: Realistic and Moderately realistic events,
• N: Somewhat realistic, Non-realistic, and Impossible events
Based on this classification, each question is assigned to one of four groups:
• Question related to empty events: No related chapter exists
• Question related to realistic events: Question relates only to chapters in class R
• Question related to non-realistic events: Question relates only to chapters in class N
• Question related to mixed events: Question relates to multiple chapters, with at least one
from each class (R and N)
This binary classification (R/N) is necessary to achieve balanced groups, as allowing more granular
combinations would lead to excessive fragmentation.
